title: Acharei Mot: not at all times (Leviticus 16:2)
hook: even the high priest may enter the holiest place only once a year

segments.voice: Yesterday, Acharei Mot began with Aaron's loss. Your line was after grief, atonement. Did an old sadness get to stay a moment? Today, the first rule of the holiest day, and the end of a week. Day four hundred six.

We live in an age of always. Stores open all night. Messages that arrive at three in the morning. Every show, every song, every person, a tap away, any hour. The idea that something should be off limits most of the time can feel almost foreign. The first instruction Moses receives for Yom Kippur isn't about what Aaron should do. It's about what he shouldn't. The most honored man in Israel, the one who wears the golden plate that says holy to the Lord, is told there's a room he may not simply walk into.
screen: `OPEN ALL NIGHT.` → `THE FIRST RULE IS A NO.` → `A ROOM HE CAN'T WALK INTO.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: tell Aaron "that he come not at all times into the holy place within the veil." Behind that curtain is the holy of holies, the ark and its cover. Second, the limit. The chapter goes on to describe one day, the tenth of the seventh month, when the high priest goes in, with incense and blood, on behalf of everyone. Only that day. The closer you are to the center, the text implies, the more the limits matter. Third, the care inside the limit. The Mishnah describes the high priest coming out of the holy of holies and saying a short prayer in the outer room. Short, it says, so as not to frighten the people waiting outside. The limit isn't coldness. Everyone outside is holding their breath for him. Fourth, the week behind us. Metzora opened with the priest going out of the camp. Then cedar and hyssop, a bird set free, a house emptied before the verdict, and a person walked home step by step. Acharei Mot began with grief before atonement. And now: not at all times. Jewish life is full of these boundaries. Shabbat closes the week's work at sundown. Some things are kept for one night a year. Many find the limit is what keeps the thing precious. A door you can open any time can stop being a door.
screen: `NOT AT ALL TIMES, BEHIND THE VEIL.` · `ONE DAY A YEAR.` · `A SHORT PRAYER, NOT TO FRIGHTEN.` · `A WEEK FROM CAMP TO SANCTUARY.` · then, large: `NOT AT ALL TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one limit. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that would mean more if it weren't available all the time. Your phone at the dinner table. A favorite food. Work email after dark. A certain conversation you keep reopening. Choose one limit you could keep, just for today, or just for this evening. Picture the door closing, gently, and what might have room to grow on the other side of it. The bell holds the time.
Acharei Mot. The portion where even the high priest may enter the holiest place only on one day a year.
Your line: not at all times. Tonight, keep one limit you chose, and notice what it protects. Day four hundred six, and another week of Leviticus behind you.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, the Musaf service in many synagogues retells the high priest's service in the holy of holies, called the Avodah, and many Jews keep limits like Shabbat rest to set time apart.

original.note: Hebrew: "at all times": from Leviticus 16:2, he may not come at all times.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old restriction on priests.
what it means: the closer you are to what's most holy, the more a limit protects it.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 16:2 limits entry behind the parochet; Mishnah Yoma 5:1 records the short prayer, not prolonged lest Israel be alarmed.

sources.quoted: that he come not at all times into the holy place within the veil

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 16:2 'that he come not at all times into the holy place within the veil' quoted from memory; confirm.
Mishnah Yoma 5:1: short prayer in the outer sanctuary so as not to alarm Israel; confirm.
The tzitz (golden plate) inscription 'holy to the Lord' (Exodus 28:36) is paraphrased in the hook.

On Yom Kippur the high priest entered the holy of holies more than once that day (Mishnah Yoma); the script says 'only that day', not 'only once'. The index hook says 'only once a year'; kept as the title's sense.
